chapters.title: Why Software Testing Matters
chapters.description: Testing as evidence, failure risks and lessons from major incidents.

questions.stem: What is the strongest general purpose of software testing?

options.text: To prove a program can never fail
To gather evidence that software behaves as intended under specified conditions
To replace requirements
To eliminate the need for design

questions.explanation: Tests provide evidence about conformance and behaviour; they cannot prove the absence of every possible defect.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: Why can software defects be especially serious in safety-critical systems?

options.text: They affect only screen colours
They can cause financial loss, injury or death
They always remain isolated to one user
They are corrected automatically

questions.explanation: Software can control physical and organisational processes, so failure consequences can extend beyond the program.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: What triggered the Ariane 5 guidance failure discussed in class?

options.text: A 16-bit integer was converted to a 64-bit float
A 64-bit floating-point value overflowed when converted to a 16-bit integer
A network cable was unplugged
The rocket ran out of fuel

questions.explanation: A value exceeded the range of the smaller integer representation, causing an unhandled overflow.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: Why did Ariane 5’s backup system not save the mission?

options.text: It used the same software and failed in the same way.
It had no access to the rocket.
It used an unrelated programming language.
It was switched off before launch by design.

questions.explanation: Identical redundant software can reproduce the same design fault, so redundancy alone did not provide independence.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: What testing gap was central to the Ariane 5 case?

options.text: The launch environment and high-speed trajectory values were not adequately simulated.
No spelling checker was used.
Only the user interface was tested.
The fuel tank was tested too often.

questions.explanation: Testing under the target flight profile could have exposed the out-of-range value before launch.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: What broader lesson follows from the Boeing MCAS example?

options.text: A technically narrow test is always enough.
Safety depends on software, sensors, organisational decisions and oversight together.
Single-sensor designs are always safer.
Regulation has no relationship to testing.

questions.explanation: System safety includes component design, sensor redundancy, operational assumptions and organisational governance.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: What caused the Patriot timing failure discussed in the lecture?

options.text: Accumulated clock drift reduced tracking accuracy.
A web route returned 404.
A database key was duplicated.
A screen resolution was unsupported.

questions.explanation: Small numerical timing errors accumulated over time and affected target tracking.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: What lesson does the CrowdStrike update example support?

options.text: Production-wide updates need representative testing and controlled rollout.
Updates should never be automated.
Only syntax errors matter.
A successful build guarantees safe deployment.

questions.explanation: A defective update can scale failure rapidly, so staged validation and rollback matter.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: What does the Rescue 117 case illustrate?

options.text: Correct code always guarantees correct outcomes.
Software can fail operationally when its underlying data is stale or incomplete.
Maps are unnecessary in aviation.
Testing cannot include data quality.

questions.explanation: A system may execute as coded yet still mislead users if critical terrain data is missing or outdated.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: Which claim about testing is most defensible?

options.text: Passing tests proves perfection.
Testing reduces uncertainty but depends on the quality and coverage of the tests.
Testing matters only after release.
Failures are caused only by programmers.

questions.explanation: Tests are evidence bounded by their assumptions, data and coverage.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: Why is testing only normal inputs inadequate?

options.text: Unexpected and boundary inputs often reveal failures hidden by typical cases.
Normal inputs are always invalid.
Boundary values cannot occur.
Testing one case proves all cases.

questions.explanation: Robustness requires cases beyond the happy path.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: What is common-mode failure in redundant software?

options.text: Two tests use different data.
Independent-looking backups fail from the same shared defect.
One backup runs faster than another.
A user repeats a request.

questions.explanation: Redundancy is weak when copies share design, code or assumptions.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: Why should operational data be part of system assurance?

options.text: Data quality matters only to databases.
Tests cannot inspect data.
Fresh data guarantees flawless code.
Correct algorithms can still produce unsafe outputs from incomplete or stale data.

questions.explanation: Software behaviour depends on both logic and the information supplied.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: What does a staged deployment reduce?

options.text: The need for rollback.
The value of monitoring.
The number of requirements.
The blast radius of a defective release.

questions.explanation: Releasing gradually limits exposure while evidence is gathered.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: Which result would most justify stopping a release?

options.text: A compiler warning unrelated to behaviour.
One user preference not in scope.
A repeatable failure on a critical acceptance condition.
A passing cosmetic test.

questions.explanation: Critical failed requirements outweigh less relevant passing checks.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: Why is relying on a single sensor dangerous in a safety-critical control system?

options.text: A single sensor always reports too slowly
Multiple sensors make software unnecessary
Sensors cannot be tested
One faulty reading can become a single point of failure

questions.explanation: Without independent corroboration, one bad signal can drive a hazardous decision.
questions.source: IS2208 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed case notes

questions.stem: What does defence in depth mean for software assurance?

options.text: Test only the most likely input
Replace all software with manual work
Use multiple independent controls so one failure does not directly cause disaster
Run the same faulty code twice

questions.explanation: Layered and sufficiently independent safeguards reduce dependence on any single control.
questions.source: IS2208 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed case notes

questions.stem: What is a fail-safe response?

options.text: The system hides the error from operators
The system always maximises throughput
On detecting an unsafe condition, the system moves towards a safer state
The system continues unchanged after every error

questions.explanation: Fail-safe behaviour prioritises safety when normal operation cannot be trusted.
questions.source: IS2208 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed case notes

questions.stem: A primary guidance computer and its backup use identical faulty assumptions. Why might both fail under the same unusual input?

options.text: A second computer removes every software defect
Redundancy makes operating conditions irrelevant
The backup necessarily uses a different specification
They share a common-mode software defect

questions.explanation: Identical assumptions can defeat apparently redundant hardware.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 1, Ariane 5 example

questions.stem: Why should a test environment use the new system’s expected operating profile?

options.text: Only source-code review can reveal overflow
Operating profiles do not affect software
Old-profile inputs may miss values and timing that occur in the new system
Realistic inputs make tests less repeatable by definition

questions.explanation: A reused component may face ranges and conditions not present in its original context.
questions.source: IS2208 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed case notes

questions.stem: What assurance practice would have reduced the risk of a faulty update reaching every machine at once?

options.text: A staged rollout with monitoring and rollback
A simultaneous global deployment
Removing all automated tests
Disabling logs

questions.explanation: Staging limits the blast radius and provides evidence before wider release.
questions.source: IS2208 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed case notes

questions.stem: Why can a tiny clock error become serious over many hours?

options.text: Repeated error accumulates into a large timing drift
Clock errors automatically cancel
Long operation reduces numerical error to zero
Timing is unrelated to tracking

questions.explanation: Small per-interval errors can accumulate until calculations are materially wrong.
questions.source: IS2208 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed case notes

questions.stem: What does stale terrain data demonstrate about system quality?

options.text: Old data are always safer than live data
Data quality matters only in finance
Correct software can still produce unsafe results when operational data are outdated
Testing source code guarantees current data

questions.explanation: Assurance must cover data currency and accuracy as well as program logic.
questions.source: IS2208 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed case notes

questions.stem: What is the key risk when reusing software in a new system?

options.text: Assumptions valid in the old context may not hold in the new one
Reused software cannot compile
Reuse always doubles performance
Reused code needs no further testing

questions.explanation: Reuse saves effort but requires revalidation against the new environment and requirements.
questions.source: IS2208 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed case notes

questions.stem: Which management decision is part of software quality, not separate from it?

options.text: Choosing whether evidence is strong enough to release
Selecting only the programming font
Avoiding all documentation
Ignoring known defects because tests are technical

questions.explanation: Release pressure, oversight and response plans affect whether technical risk reaches users.
questions.source: IS2208 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed case notes

chapters.title: Test-First Thinking, Requirements & Evidence
chapters.description: Tests as executable specifications, test quality and iterative validation.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a test-first approach?

options.text: Implementation is completed before requirements are considered.
Tests expressing expected behaviour are written before the implementation.
Testing is delegated only to users.
Only manual inspection is permitted.

questions.explanation: Test-first development turns requirements into tests before code is written to satisfy them.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: Why can a system pass tests and still be wrong?

options.text: Tests may encode an incorrect standard or omit important behaviour.
Passing automatically changes the requirements.
Compilers ignore every test.
A passing result means the code did not run.

questions.explanation: Test results are only as trustworthy as the test design, oracle and coverage.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: What did the Hubble mirror case demonstrate?

options.text: Accurate manufacturing makes tests unnecessary.
A faulty test instrument can certify a faulty product.
Space hardware cannot be tested.
Independent checks always agree.

questions.explanation: The mirror matched a miscalibrated reference, so it passed the wrong standard.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: What makes a requirement testable?

options.text: It states an observable condition that can be checked.
It uses vague words such as “good”.
It avoids measurable outcomes.
It depends on the tester’s mood.

questions.explanation: A testable requirement defines behaviour or acceptance conditions that evidence can verify.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: If direct testing of a requirement is impossible, what is the best course?

options.text: Ignore the requirement.
Use justified indirect evidence or a proxy and state its limits.
Declare the feature correct.
Replace it with an unrelated test.

questions.explanation: Indirect evidence can support a claim when direct observation is impossible, but its assumptions must be explicit.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: In the shooting-project example, why was real field data important?

options.text: It exposed differences between assumptions and actual operating conditions.
It eliminated the need for tests.
It guaranteed every future shot.
It made implementation unnecessary.

questions.explanation: Real observations help refine both the model and the tests when laboratory assumptions are incomplete.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: What is the value of iterating from data to tests to implementation and back to field validation?

options.text: Each cycle can reveal faulty assumptions and improve the specification.
It prevents requirements from changing.
It replaces evidence with intuition.
It ensures the first design is retained.

questions.explanation: Iterative validation allows the model, tests and code to improve in response to evidence.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: What problem can “backwards logic” create in a detection system?

options.text: It can make the system appear successful by interpreting outcomes through the desired conclusion.
It always reduces false positives.
It guarantees causal evidence.
It removes the need for thresholds.

questions.explanation: Reasoning from a desired answer can produce circular validation and false positives.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: Which is the best test oracle?

options.text: A clearly specified expected result
The implementation’s current output
A random value
The most recent user guess

questions.explanation: An oracle states what the correct outcome should be independently of the code under test.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: Why should tests be reviewed like production code?

options.text: Defects in tests can conceal defects in the implementation.
Tests cannot contain logic.
Reviewing tests slows all learning.
Only production code affects quality.

questions.explanation: Incorrect assertions, data or assumptions can give false confidence.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: Which requirement is most testable?

options.text: The code should be modern.
The response is returned within two seconds for the stated workload.
The system should be very fast.
The interface should feel nice.

questions.explanation: A measurable threshold and conditions define observable acceptance.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: What is a false positive in a detection system?

options.text: The system reports a target when none is present.
The system misses a real target.
A test fails before implementation.
A compiler rejects invalid syntax.

questions.explanation: A positive detection is false when the claimed condition is absent.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: What is a false negative?

options.text: An input is converted to an integer.
The system fails to report a condition that is present.
The system reports a condition that is absent.
Every test passes.

questions.explanation: A negative result is false when the real condition exists.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: Why should an expected result be independent of the implementation?

options.text: Otherwise the test may repeat the same mistake as the code.
Implementations cannot produce outputs.
Independent results are always random.
Tests must avoid requirements.

questions.explanation: An oracle derived from the code can create circular validation.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: What should happen when field evidence contradicts a passing test suite?

options.text: Revisit the assumptions, requirements and tests as well as the implementation.
Ignore the field evidence.
Declare the environment invalid automatically.
Delete the failing observations.

questions.explanation: Real evidence can reveal gaps in the model or coverage.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: In test-first development, what should exist before the production behaviour is implemented?

options.text: An executable example of the expected behaviour
A completed user interface
A deployment to all users
A performance optimisation plan

questions.explanation: Writing the test first clarifies the requirement and defines evidence of success.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 and reviewed project notes

questions.stem: Why is “the system should be user-friendly” a weak test requirement?

options.text: It is too numerical
It names a system user
It can be compiled
It lacks a measurable condition and agreed success criterion

questions.explanation: Vague qualities need operational definitions before they can be tested consistently.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 and reviewed project notes

questions.stem: Which is the most testable rewrite of “the page should be fast”?

options.text: The page should feel reasonably quick
The page should use modern code
The page should never wait
The page should return the specified response within 500 ms under the stated test load

questions.explanation: A threshold plus defined conditions creates an observable pass/fail rule.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 and reviewed project notes

questions.stem: A developer copies a flawed calculation into both production code and the expected-value expression. What can a passing test conceal?

options.text: The same mistake in both the implementation and test
A complete absence of executable assertions
A guaranteed failure of every correct function
A proof that the requirement was satisfied

questions.explanation: An independent expected value reduces the risk of shared implementation mistakes.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 9, independent expectations

questions.stem: What is direct evidence that an age rule “21 or older is allowed” works?

options.text: Tests at 20, 21 and 22 produce the specified decisions
The function name contains age
A developer says the code looks right
The program starts without syntax errors

questions.explanation: Observed boundary behaviour directly checks the rule.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 and reviewed project notes

questions.stem: When direct measurement is impossible, what makes indirect evidence credible?

options.text: A colourful report
Use of the same code as the implementation
A justified chain linking the proxy measurement to the requirement
A large number of unrelated tests

questions.explanation: Indirect evidence must show why the proxy genuinely supports the claim.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 and reviewed project notes

questions.stem: Why was calibrated test equipment central to the Hubble lesson?

options.text: Multiple measurements are always independent
A wrong measuring instrument can validate a wrongly manufactured component
Calibration affects only software speed
The mirror had no requirement

questions.explanation: If the reference itself is wrong, repeated agreement can still support the wrong conclusion.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 and reviewed project notes

questions.stem: A detector raises many alarms for harmless events. Which quality problem is dominant?

options.text: A high false-positive rate
A high false-negative rate
A syntax error
A missing route

questions.explanation: False positives label normal cases as detections and can make the system unusable.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 and reviewed project notes

questions.stem: A detector misses real events but rarely raises false alarms. Which quality problem is dominant?

options.text: A high false-positive rate
Excessive code comments
A dependency conflict
A high false-negative rate

questions.explanation: False negatives occur when actual target events are not detected.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 and reviewed project notes

questions.stem: What should happen when a requirement changes?

options.text: Delete the whole test suite
Change only the test result labels
Update the relevant tests and implementation while preserving evidence for unchanged behaviour
Keep old tests and ignore the new requirement

questions.explanation: Tests act as an executable specification and must evolve deliberately with requirements.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 2 and reviewed project notes

chapters.title: Components, Integration & System Testing
chapters.description: Testing levels, the S-Plan heating example and diagnostic strategy.

questions.stem: What does component testing focus on?

options.text: Individual units or parts in isolation
The complete organisation
Only live customers
Unrelated external systems

questions.explanation: Component tests check the behaviour of a single part before relying on its interactions.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: What does integration testing focus on?

options.text: Whether connected components work together correctly
Whether one function compiles
Only user satisfaction
Only hardware temperature

questions.explanation: Integration testing examines interfaces and collaborations between components.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: What does system testing focus on?

options.text: The complete assembled system against its intended behaviour
One variable in one function only
The spelling of class names
Individual components without interaction

questions.explanation: System tests assess end-to-end behaviour of the whole system.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: In the S-Plan heating example, when should a zone valve open?

options.text: When the timer is on and the thermostat calls for heat
Whenever the boiler is off
Only when every thermostat is satisfied
Whenever a browser route is requested

questions.explanation: The controls combine schedule and temperature demand before opening the relevant flow path.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: Why is a flow-path interlock important before starting the boiler and pump?

options.text: It helps prevent operation without a valid route for water flow.
It increases the web-server port.
It hides error messages.
It converts strings to integers.

questions.explanation: The interlock is a safety condition confirming that the system can circulate water.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: When building a known system from parts, what is a sensible testing sequence?

options.text: Component, then integration, then system testing
System testing only
Deployment, then requirements
Random testing with no component checks

questions.explanation: Testing builds confidence progressively from parts to interactions and the complete system.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: When diagnosing an unfamiliar failed system, why might testing start at the whole-system level?

options.text: A broad symptom can identify which subsystem should be isolated next.
Component tests are illegal.
The architecture never matters.
Whole-system tests reveal every internal line automatically.

questions.explanation: Troubleshooting may begin with the observed failure and narrow down to components.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: What is black-box testing?

options.text: Testing behaviour through inputs and outputs without relying on internal implementation
Inspecting only source-code style
Testing with the screen turned off
Running no test data

questions.explanation: Black-box tests evaluate externally visible behaviour against a specification.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: Why can architecture knowledge improve testing even when black-box tests are used?

options.text: It helps identify interfaces, states and combinations likely to fail.
It makes expected results unnecessary.
It proves implementation correctness.
It prevents system testing.

questions.explanation: Knowledge of structure guides coverage and diagnosis without replacing behavioural checks.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: Why are both component and whole-system tests necessary?

options.text: Parts can pass alone yet fail when combined, while whole-system tests may not localise defects.
They always test identical behaviour.
System tests make interfaces irrelevant.
Component tests cover every environment.

questions.explanation: The levels answer different questions and complement each other.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: Two components pass alone but fail when connected. Which test level exposed the issue?

options.text: Static formatting
Requirements elicitation only
Integration testing
Component testing only

questions.explanation: The defect lies in their interface or interaction.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: A complete heating system reaches the wrong room temperature despite working components. Which test is most relevant?

options.text: Package installation
One isolated valve test only
System testing
A syntax check

questions.explanation: End-to-end behaviour must be checked against the system requirement.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: Why can a system test be poor at locating a defect?

options.text: It tests only one function.
It provides no expected result.
It observes a broad failure involving many possible components.
It never executes code.

questions.explanation: Whole-system evidence confirms failure but often needs narrower tests for diagnosis.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: What is white-box testing?

options.text: Testing only visible outputs without implementation knowledge.
Reviewing user colours.
Running production without tests.
Designing tests with knowledge of internal paths and structure.

questions.explanation: White-box coverage uses internal implementation information.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: What is an interface contract?

options.text: A replacement for system requirements.
An agreed format and behaviour governing component interaction.
A licence to sell hardware.
A user-interface colour guide only.

questions.explanation: Integration depends on components sharing compatible expectations.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: In the S-Plan example, what two conditions normally create a call for heat in a zone?

options.text: The timer permits heating and the thermostat detects demand
The pump is off and the bypass is closed
Both zone valves are permanently open
The boiler is already hot

questions.explanation: The schedule and temperature requirement jointly determine whether the zone should request heat.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 and S-Plan heating example

questions.stem: What confirms that a motorised zone valve has opened before the boiler and pump run?

options.text: The room colour
The database schema
The thermostat battery label
Its end-switch signal

questions.explanation: The valve end switch provides evidence that a flow path is open.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 and S-Plan heating example

questions.stem: Why is a bypass path useful in a heating system?

options.text: It protects flow when normal zone paths are restricted or closing
It increases every thermostat setting
It replaces the boiler controller
It guarantees perfect room temperature

questions.explanation: A bypass helps maintain safe circulation rather than forcing the pump against closed paths.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 and S-Plan heating example

questions.stem: A thermostat passes its bench test, but the valve never opens when heat is requested. What should be tested next?

options.text: The interface and control path between thermostat and valve
Only the boiler fuel supply
The room paint colour
The thermostat again with the same isolated setup

questions.explanation: The defect may lie in wiring, signals or interaction rather than either component alone.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 and S-Plan heating example

questions.stem: Why can all components pass individually while the system fails?

options.text: Component tests prove every interaction
System tests are unnecessary
Interfaces cannot contain defects
Correct parts can still interact through incorrect signals, timing or configuration

questions.explanation: Integration behaviour depends on connections and coordination that isolated tests do not exercise.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 and S-Plan heating example

questions.stem: Which is an acceptance-style system test for the heating example?

options.text: A wire has continuity
The thermostat display lights
Under stated room and timer conditions, the correct zones reach the required temperatures safely
The valve motor rotates on a bench

questions.explanation: A system-level test checks the complete user-visible outcome under realistic conditions.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 and S-Plan heating example

questions.stem: When troubleshooting an unfamiliar installed system, why might a top-down approach be efficient?

options.text: Every component must be replaced first
Architecture knowledge is harmful
System behaviour never reveals location clues
A failing whole-system symptom can narrow which subsystem needs investigation

questions.explanation: Starting from symptoms and tracing inward avoids testing unrelated parts blindly.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 and S-Plan heating example

questions.stem: What is combinatorial explosion in system testing?

options.text: Components physically explode under load
Every test returns the same result
Testing one case generates all other cases automatically
The number of possible state and input combinations grows too large to test exhaustively

questions.explanation: Interactions among many variables create far more combinations than practical test time allows.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 and S-Plan heating example

questions.stem: How should risk guide selection when exhaustive testing is impossible?

options.text: Ignore rare but catastrophic failures
Prioritise high-impact failures, likely scenarios and critical interfaces
Test only the easiest path
Choose cases alphabetically

questions.explanation: Risk-based testing allocates effort where failure would matter most.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 and S-Plan heating example

questions.stem: What does white-box knowledge add to black-box testing?

options.text: It removes the need for requirements
It limits tests to user-interface colours
It helps choose cases that exercise important branches, states and interfaces
It guarantees the absence of defects

questions.explanation: Internal knowledge can improve coverage while outcomes are still checked externally.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 3 and S-Plan heating example

chapters.title: Python, Environments & Flask Basics
chapters.description: Python setup, virtual environments, Flask applications and routes.

questions.stem: What does it mean that Python is interpreted in the course context?

options.text: Code can be executed interactively without a separate manual compile step.
Python code never has syntax rules.
Python is always faster than native code.
Python cannot use libraries.

questions.explanation: The interpreter supports quick execution and experimentation, though performance can differ from compiled code.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: Which command checks the installed Python version?

options.text: python -V
python install
pip route
flask -Q

questions.explanation: python -V reports the interpreter version.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: Why use a virtual environment for a Python project?

options.text: To isolate project dependencies from other projects and the system installation
To host the public website automatically
To remove Python from the computer
To prevent tests from running

questions.explanation: An isolated environment reduces dependency conflicts and improves reproducibility.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: What does pip freeze help record?

options.text: Installed package versions in the current environment
All Flask routes
Expected test results
The operating system password

questions.explanation: It lists installed dependencies and versions that can be captured for reproducibility.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: What is Flask?

options.text: A lightweight Python web framework
A database query language
A unit-test assertion
A hardware simulator

questions.explanation: Flask provides routing and web-server facilities for Python applications.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: What is the usual role of @app.route("/") in a basic Flask application?

options.text: Map the root URL to a Python function
Create a virtual environment
Install PyTest
Convert every input to an integer

questions.explanation: The decorator registers the URL path handled by the following function.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: What should a simple Flask route function return?

options.text: A response value such as a string
A package installation command
Only a class definition
A compiler executable

questions.explanation: Flask converts the returned value into the HTTP response.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: What address does 127.0.0.1 normally refer to?

options.text: The local machine
Every public website
The DNS root server
A remote database

questions.explanation: The loopback address allows the developer to access a locally running server.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: Why must Flask endpoint function names be unique within the application?

options.text: Flask uses them to identify endpoints and duplicate names can conflict.
Python forbids all repeated words.
Unique names improve internet speed.
Routes cannot contain slashes otherwise.

questions.explanation: Endpoint identity is derived from the function unless configured otherwise.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: Why test a custom Sums class before connecting it to a Flask route?

options.text: It separates business-logic defects from web-integration defects.
Flask can never call classes.
Unit tests require a browser.
The route will compile the class automatically.

questions.explanation: Testing the class in isolation makes failures easier to locate before integration.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: Why pin dependency versions for a project?

options.text: To convert Python into HTML.
To guarantee zero defects.
To make installations more reproducible across machines and time.
To prevent any package use.

questions.explanation: Recorded versions reduce unexpected behaviour from dependency changes.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: What is the purpose of if __name__ == "__main__" in a simple Flask file?

options.text: Install the virtual environment.
Create a test assertion.
Run startup code when the file is executed directly.
Declare every route.

questions.explanation: The guard distinguishes direct execution from import.
questions.source: IS2208 Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: Why keep business logic outside route functions where practical?
